And these are the Avestas, which is the Bible of Zoroastrianism, and Hinduism in India, which gave birth to Hinduism. We'll discuss this later in the semester but I want you to be aware of it. Again, we know that this happened first because of linguistic studies. When we looked at different languages, we discovered common words like "father": Latin is *pater*, Greek is *pater*, Persian is *padar*, Hindi is *pitā*. Pretty similar. "Mother" in Latin is *mater*, Greek is *mētēr*, Persian is *madar*, and Hindi is *mā*. So from different linguistic studies, we know they had a common language.

In another stark example of the Proto-Indo-European (PIE) language, the dual form exists. You can see how it spreads to other languages in the PIE family: "dua" in PIE becomes "tua" in Latin and "two" in English. So all these languages are interrelated. That's why if you speak one like English, it's pretty easy for you to learn the other languages as well. Whereas if you speak Chinese, it doesn't really help you when you go learn other languages.

Linguists have done studies of words that are distinct to Proto-Indo-European (PIE) and these are the words they discovered: *bów* (cow), *ox*, *ram*, *eel*, *dog*, *grain*, *cauldron*, *wrestling*, *wealth*, *households*, *families*, *clans*. These words are unique to their culture, and therefore, we're able to group these words together and discover four characteristics: First, they have lots of words for the wheel. They also have dairy terms but no farming terms, and they have words for horse. That's why we can figure out that these are nomadic pastoralists from the steppes.

Through archaeology and DNA studies, we get a better understanding of who they were. They had to be past because of the way they use words. So let's talk about old Europe before the Yamnayans came and conquered them. This is Marija Gimbutas, an American Lithuanian anthropologist, who was the first to hypothesize that old Europe must have been conquered by these people. She did a lot of archaeology and discovered their culture was primarily peaceful, honored women, and exposed ego-arianism—exactly what I said previously. The Yamnayans were different; they were patriarchal, property holders, and very aggressive.

Maria Gimbutas wrote many books like "The Language of the Goddess," which is amazing. So if you have a chance, please study her work. This mother goddess of civilization was a symbol of the unity of all life in nature. Her power was in water, stone, tomb, cave, animals, birds, snakes, fish, hills, trees, and flowers. Therefore, this culture had a holistic and mythopoetic perception of the sacredness and mystery of everything on earth.

This is a religion that practices balance and harmony because everything is sacred. You cannot destroy life without first getting permission from the mother goddess. This culture took deep delight in the natural wonders of the world. Their people did not produce lethal weapons or build forts in unacceptable places as their successors did even when they were acquainted with metallurgy. Instead, they built magnificent tombs, shrines, and temples, comfortable houses in moderately-sized villages, and created superb pottery and sculptures. This was a long-lasting period of remarkable creativity and stability without strife.

Their culture was a culture of art. They don't fight; they are egalitarian. They practice art. And what's really important for us to understand is that they had writing systems and technology but chose not to use it for war because it was against their religion. They also had writing systems and symbols, something Márja Gimbutas has done a lot of research on. When the Yamnayans came, they completely inverted the culture. For example, old Europeans believed that the snake symbolized life energy and regeneration.
